title: Money that reaches City-funded organizations through a go-between
question: Which funders pay fiscal sponsors, community foundations and other grant-making bodies that in turn pay City-funded organizations, and where can the chain be followed by name?
finding: 66 go-betweens received $1.86 billion from the funders on file in 2020 to 2025 and themselves granted $930.5 million to City-paid organizations; the largest by money received are Silicon Valley Community Foundation ($319.8 million in, $243.3 million on to City-paid organizations); Tides Center ($227.6 million in, $41.0 million on to City-paid organizations); The San Francisco Foundation ($209.7 million in, $196.9 million on to City-paid organizations); California Community Foundation ($118.5 million in, $49.6 million on to City-paid organizations). In 2 funder-and-go-between pairs ($5.3 million) the first grant's printed purpose names a City-paid organization that the go-between also paid, so the chain can be read from the two returns: Crankstart Foundation through The San Francisco Foundation (The SF Housing Accelerator Fund); The San Francisco Foundation through Asian Amer Advncng Jstc-Asian Law Caucus (Chinese For Affirmative Action). A further $5.67 billion in 589 grants went to four national donor-advised-fund sponsors whose own returns are not on disk; where that money went next cannot be followed here.
how: A go-between is (a) a City-paid organization whose own Form 990 Schedule I (its list of grants made) shows grants to other City-paid organizations, or (b) a community foundation or other public-charity grantmaker in the funders' file. First leg: grants to it from the other funders on file, 2020 to 2025. Second leg: its own grants to City-paid organizations, where those come to $100,000 or more over the same years. A chain is 'followed by name' when the first grant's printed purpose contains the name (three words or more) of a City-paid organization the go-between also paid. Rows are funder and go-between pairs with a first leg of $25,000 or more; named chains come first, then the pairs where the smaller of the two legs is largest.
limits: Giving through a community foundation, a donor-advised fund (an account whose donor recommends the grants) or a fiscal sponsor (an established charity that receives money for projects it hosts) is routine. Except where a purpose names the final recipient, the two legs are not the same dollars: a go-between pools money from many sources, so the second-leg column is everything it sent on, not this funder's share. Because the same dollar appears in the first funder's return and again in the go-between's, adding the two legs double-counts. Grants a City-funded organization makes onward are also covered in the onward-grants page.
